clue.text: Seconds: extremely cheap and most delicious

parts.note: S is the stopwatch abbreviation for seconds
crummy means cheap and shoddy, and pushed to its extreme the adjective goes into its superlative form

explanation.surface: A diner goes back for second helpings of food that was dirt cheap and utterly delicious.
explanation.walkthrough: The colon invites you to read the first word as a second helping, which the definition at the far end is only too happy to encourage. It is a stopwatch abbreviation.
explanation.definitionFit: most delicious: the superlative of 'scrummy', a nursery shortening of scrumptious, so it names food at the very top of tasty.

clue.text: Primarily solve / understand (somewhat slangily!)

indicators.note: To do something primarily is to do it first of all, so each word after it yields only the letter it begins with.

parts.note: the starting letters of the four words, taken in the order they stand

explanation.surface: A teacher's aside on the main point: work it out and grasp it, put informally.
explanation.walkthrough: An all-in-one: the very words that hand over their opening letters also describe what the answer means, and the exclamation mark is the setter flagging the informal register.
explanation.definitionFit: The whole clue reads straight: to work something out or grasp it, in casual British speech, is precisely what this verb means.

clue.text: Regretted being audibly crass

indicators.note: What is audible reaches you through the ear, so the word beside it is to be taken by its sound and then written down another way.

parts.note: a crass remark is a rude one, and out loud the two spellings are impossible to tell apart

explanation.surface: Someone wishes they had not said something so vulgar out loud.
explanation.walkthrough: Past tense on both sides: the definition is in the past, so what you hear has to be written down as a past tense too, which is what makes the odd spelling findable.
explanation.definitionFit: Regretted: to rue something is to look back on it with sorrow, a verb that survives mainly in the phrase 'rue the day'.

clue.text: Everyman broadcast main goal: modicum of admiration (a delusion)

parts.note: the setter refers to himself, so Everyman gives me

indicators.note: broadcast seed is scattered widely, so these letters are scattered into a new order

parts.note: taken as written, as anagram material

indicators.note: a modicum is a tiny amount, here just the first letter

parts.note: only its first letter is wanted

explanation.surface: The setter announces his chief aim: a little admiration.
explanation.walkthrough: A setter naming himself means ME. 'broadcast' scrambles ME with MAIN GOAL to give MEGALOMANI, and the A from 'modicum of admiration' completes it.
explanation.definitionFit: Megalomania is an obsessive belief in one's own power or greatness, a delusion of grandeur.

clue.text: Wine Kit's drunk: that's no shock

indicators.note: drunk means intoxicated and unsteady, so the letters stagger into a new order

explanation.surface: Kit has been at the wine again, which surprises nobody.
explanation.walkthrough: 'drunk' rearranges WINE and KIT; the 's is 'is', joining them to the signal.
explanation.definitionFit: Saying 'I knew it' expresses that an outcome was expected, so it comes as no surprise.

clue.text: Suspends from ledges

definitions.meaning: in the sense of putting a plan on hold, not of hanging something from a hook
the plural noun: flat boards fixed to a wall, named after the rock ledges they imitate

explanation.walkthrough: Three words, two definitions and nothing else: 'from' is joinery, and a solver hunting a mechanism inside these seven letters will find none.
explanation.definitionFit: Suspends is the verb, putting a plan on hold; ledges is the plural noun, the boards a wall carries. One word, two parts of speech.

clue.text: Making comeback, builds upon incomplete work

indicators.note: Something making a comeback returns the way it went, so this run of letters is read against the direction the entry travels.
The words on either side are not used whole: each gives up only the end or the start of itself to the run.

parts.note: four letters straddle the gap between the two words, and they are read from right to left

explanation.surface: A builder back on the job adds to a half-finished project.
explanation.walkthrough: 'work' looks like part of the surface picture — an unfinished job — and a solver who reads it that way has the right words in the wrong roles.
explanation.definitionFit: work: a composer's numbered piece is called exactly that, which is why concert programmes print Op. in front of its number.

clue.text: Performs at resort in which it's always cold

indicators.note: read as re-sort, to sort again, so the letters are arranged afresh

explanation.surface: An entertainer does a show at a holiday resort where it is permanently freezing.
explanation.walkthrough: 'resort' looks like a holiday destination but is read as re-sort, the signal to rearrange PERFORMS AT.
explanation.definitionFit: Permafrost is ground that stays frozen all year round, in polar regions.

clue.text: What could be represented as 'eats mice'?

definitions.text: What could be represented as 'eats mice'?

parts.words: What could be represented as 'eats mice'?
parts.note: a description of a pet by its habit: a domestic feline breed whose job, proverbially, is catching and eating mice

explanation.walkthrough: The quoted phrase looks like anagram fodder, but its letters do not make the answer; the clue simply describes the animal by what it does.
explanation.definitionFit: A Siamese is a pale, blue-eyed breed of domestic feline, and felines are famous for catching mice.

clue.text: Repress redhead that's spicy in the kitchen

definitions.note: The definition is an adjective phrase where a noun is wanted: the setter is describing the ingredient rather than offering a word you could swap straight in.

parts.note: to stem a flow or a tide is to hold it back
British slang for a person with red hair, from the colour of the root

explanation.surface: A fiery red-haired cook is told to hold back their temper in the kitchen.
explanation.walkthrough: Both halves are ordinary words in kitchen clothes: a verb about holding something back and a nickname for hair colour, edible only once they are pushed together.
explanation.definitionFit: The definition describes rather than substitutes: the preserved root sold in syrup is a baking-cupboard staple with a hot, peppery bite.

clue.text: Guard's van regularly out of service: bear up?

indicators.note: every other letter is put out of service at regular intervals, leaving the alternate ones

parts.note: only the second, fourth, sixth and eighth letters of these words are used

explanation.surface: A railway guard's van is often out of action.
explanation.walkthrough: Take the even letters of GUARDSVAN. The question mark marks the definition: Ursa, the bear, is found 'up' in the sky as a constellation.
explanation.definitionFit: Ursa is Latin for bear and names the constellations Ursa Major and Minor, so it is a bear up in the heavens.

clue.text: Divorcées getting dog, we're told: it may not be true

parts.note: a divorcée is a former wife, and former wives are old ones — two words the wordplay uses whole

indicators.note: What we are told arrives as sound, so one piece has to be written down as a different word that happens to sound the same.

parts.note: the part of a dog that wags; spoken, it is indistinguishable from the word that gets written down

explanation.surface: Gossip says the divorced wives got the dog in the settlement, though the story may be untrue.
explanation.walkthrough: The first word does the heavy lifting: former wives are old wives, an idiom rather than an insult. The colon is all that separates wordplay from definition.
explanation.definitionFit: it may not be true: the phrase names a piece of traditional lore passed on as fact, and the whole force of the label is that it is unreliable.

clue.text: 'Bird watching' is one for these?

parts.note: swap the opening sounds of bird watching and you get word batching, a batch of words, which is the sort of swap named after the Reverend Spooner

explanation.walkthrough: The clue reads like a hobby enquiry, but bird watching with its first sounds exchanged becomes word batching, the classic transposition attributed to William Spooner of Oxford.
explanation.definitionFit: A spoonerism is a slip that swaps the initial sounds of two words, so 'word batching' for bird watching would be one.

clue.text: Interlaced characters arranged for an entitlement

indicators.note: the characters, the letters, of interlaced are arranged into a new order

explanation.surface: A document with interlaced lettering is set out as proof of someone's rights.
explanation.walkthrough: 'characters arranged' says the letters of INTERLACED are reordered; 'for' is the link.
explanation.definitionFit: A credential is a qualification or document giving someone a right or title, an entitlement.

clue.text: Note describing quarrel over grain in vessel

indicators.note: in a down clue over means placed above what follows
describing in its old sense of drawing round, so the note encloses the arrow

parts.note: NB, nota bene, is a written note
a quarrel is a bolt shot from a crossbow, a kind of arrow
oat is a cereal grain

explanation.surface: A note describes an argument over grain aboard a ship.
explanation.walkthrough: 'quarrel' looks like an argument but is the crossbow bolt, ARROW, held inside NB.
explanation.definitionFit: A narrowboat is a long thin canal boat, a kind of watercraft.

clue.text: Let back in to study at Cambridge University

parts.note: at a British university you read a subject rather than major in it
the Massachusetts Institute of Technology stands in Cambridge, across the river from Boston

explanation.surface: A student is allowed back to resume a degree at Cambridge.
explanation.walkthrough: The trap is the other Cambridge. The surface points firmly at the English university town, and the institute the setter means is the one in Massachusetts.
explanation.definitionFit: Let back in: to admit someone a second time is to let them in again, the prefix carrying the 'back' of the definition.

clue.text: Anathema: jerk takes over company

indicators.note: One firm taking over another swallows it whole, so the shorter piece ends up inside the longer rather than after it.

parts.note: a jerk and a surge are both a sudden movement forward
CO is the abbreviation printed after a firm's name

explanation.surface: Staff are horrified when an obnoxious boss seizes control of their firm.
explanation.walkthrough: The colon reads as a definition mark, and it is one. 'takes over' looks like a business manoeuvre, which is exactly the surface the setter is paying for.
explanation.definitionFit: Anathema: something loathed and cursed, and the answer names a plague or affliction that blights whatever it touches, so both nouns name a thing wished away.

clue.text: Led government that's welcomed by pair in Mexican city

indicators.note: A host who welcomes guests takes them indoors, so the pair opens up and receives the other letters between its own.

parts.note: a duo is two of anything, most often two performers
to run a company is to lead it, and the tense matches
G is the one-letter abbreviation for government

explanation.surface: A two-person team greets the leader of a new administration in a Mexican city.
explanation.walkthrough: Durango is a city in northern Mexico and the state around it. 'Led' wants to begin a sentence about a leader; it is a three-letter past tense doing wordplay.
explanation.definitionFit: Mexican city: the answer is the capital of the Mexican state of the same name, so the definition is plain geography with no trickery in it.

clue.text: Act dictatorially towards operation by newspapers

parts.note: OP is the hospital shorthand for an operation
the press is the collective name for newspapers and the people who write them

explanation.surface: The papers behave like tyrants over a covert operation they are reporting.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface is a medical procedure covered by the papers, and that is where the join hides: the little word between the two halves is joinery and carries no letters.
explanation.definitionFit: Act dictatorially towards: the verb means to rule harshly and keep a people down, which is precisely how a dictator behaves towards those under them.

clue.text: Forgetting a name is awkward

indicators.note: awkward means clumsy, so the letters are clumsily rearranged

explanation.surface: Not remembering someone's name is socially embarrassing.
explanation.walkthrough: 'awkward' rearranges A NAME IS.
explanation.definitionFit: Amnesia is loss of memory, the condition of failing to remember.

clue.text: A quiet time, breeze regularly blowing in bit of woodland

parts.note: the clue's own letter, taken exactly as it stands
the noise you make when asking for silence
T is the standard abbreviation for time

indicators.note: Taken regularly means taken at an even interval, so every second letter of the word is picked up and the rest left behind.

parts.note: every second letter of the word, counting from its second

explanation.surface: A calm spell in a small wood, with a light wind gusting through now and then.
explanation.walkthrough: Four pieces for seven letters, and the smallest of them is the bare letter that opens the clue — easy to read as an article and skip straight past.
explanation.definitionFit: bit of woodland: one tree is a piece of what a wood is made of, so the definition names the answer by the larger thing it belongs to.

clue.text: Ashen, whimper pathetically somewhere in the USA

indicators.note: pathetically means feebly and pitifully, so the letters collapse into a new order

explanation.surface: Pale-faced, someone whimpers miserably on a trip to America.
explanation.walkthrough: 'pathetically' rearranges ASHEN WHIMPER.
explanation.definitionFit: New Hampshire is one of the six New England states in the north-eastern United States.

clue.text: Bertie and Rosemary?

definitions.meaning: one familiar shortening of a long forename; the four letters wanted are another shortening of that same name
a plant grown for flavouring, so this half defines by example — which is what the question mark admits

explanation.walkthrough: Two proper names and no wordplay at all: one is a person, one is a plant, and the question mark covers both for being examples rather than equivalents.
explanation.definitionFit: Bertie and the answer are both pet forms of Herbert; rosemary is one example of the kitchen plants the noun covers, which the question mark flags.

clue.text: Ocular irritant in some dusty environs

indicators.note: Some of a thing is a portion of it, and a portion of a phrase means a run of its letters rather than any part of its meaning.

parts.note: four letters run without a break from inside the first word into the start of the second

explanation.surface: Something irritating the eyes in grimy, dusty surroundings.
explanation.walkthrough: The definition works hard to look like the surface's subject — grit blown into the eye — while the letters sit in plain view across the final two words.
explanation.definitionFit: Ocular irritant: the small inflamed swelling on an eyelid is exactly that, something at the eye that hurts and will not be ignored.

clue.text: Sample from Antipodean music held here

definitions.note: The setter defines by description, not by synonym: a noun is wanted and what the clue offers is a phrase saying what the thing is for.

indicators.note: A sample is a small piece cut out of something bigger, so a run of letters is lifted straight out of the long word that follows.

parts.note: four consecutive letters sit inside the long word, beginning at its second letter

explanation.surface: A clip of Australian music is stored at this spot.
explanation.walkthrough: The capital letter and the Australian angle are the misdirection, and the word is long enough that the four letters buried inside it go unnoticed.
explanation.definitionFit: music held here: the pocket player stores a library of songs, so the phrase points at the object by the job it does rather than by a synonym.

clue.text: Reports, etc. edited in contemplation of the past

indicators.note: edited means revised and reworked, so the letters are put into a new order

explanation.surface: Old reports and the like are revised by a historian looking back.
explanation.walkthrough: 'edited' rearranges REPORTS ETC; 'in' is the link to the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: Retrospect is a review of past events, as in the phrase 'in retrospect'.

clue.text: And others sent back behind

indicators.note: Something sent back travels the way it came, so the four letters are read from the far end towards the near one.

parts.note: et al is the Latin tag a bibliography uses for the authors it cannot be bothered to list

explanation.surface: The rest of the group are made to return to the rear.
explanation.walkthrough: The definition means behind time, not behind in space: a runner behind the field is the wrong picture, a train behind schedule the right one.
explanation.definitionFit: behind: in the sense of behind schedule rather than behind in space, which is how a train or a payment earns the word.

clue.text: So-called noblesse — it's dubious

indicators.note: dubious means doubtful or shady, so the letters are not to be trusted in their order

explanation.surface: The supposed nobility of the upper classes is questionable.
explanation.walkthrough: 'dubious' rearranges NOBLESSE and IT; the 's is 'is', linking them to the signal.
explanation.definitionFit: Ostensible means apparent or professed, stated but perhaps not real, like so-called.
